definition.text: A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off.

facts.text: A Pareto improvement is a change that leaves at least one person better off and nobody worse off; Pareto efficiency is reached once no such change is left.
Example: if Smith owns an apple but wants an orange, and Jones owns an orange but wants an apple, the situation is inefficient because trading makes both better off.
It is named after Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and income distribution.
Pareto called it 'optimal', but it does not pick one best outcome; it only marks out a set of outcomes, which is why 'efficiency' fits better.
Pareto efficiency does not mean fairness: an economy where a wealthy few hold most resources can still be Pareto efficient.
Market failure is a case where markets do not produce an efficient allocation, so a Pareto improvement is possible.
In social choice theory the same idea is called the unanimity principle: if everyone prefers A to B, society should too.

Because asymmetric information, adverse selection and moral hazard make Pareto efficiency hard to judge in practice, most people do not take the welfare theorems as accurate descriptions of the real world.

definition.text: A situation is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off.

facts.text: A strong Pareto improvement makes all agents strictly better off, while an ordinary Pareto improvement needs only one strictly better off and the rest no worse.
Every strong Pareto improvement is also a weak one, but not the reverse, so a weakly efficient outcome may not be fully Pareto efficient.

definition.text: A weaker form of Pareto efficiency that recognises a planner such as a government may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome because it faces the same limits as everyone else.

facts.text: It matters when people hold private information, such as a worker's own productivity or a used car's quality, leading to moral hazard or adverse selection.
A planner usually has no more information than market participants, so it can only use anonymous rules or rules based on observable behaviour.
If no allowed rule can improve on the market outcome, that outcome is called constrained Pareto optimal.

definition.text: The link showing that maximizing a weighted sum of everyone's utility, with positive weights, always gives a Pareto efficient allocation, and under some assumptions every efficient allocation can be found that way.

facts.text: An allocation that maximizes a positively weighted sum of utilities must be Pareto efficient, since any Pareto improvement would raise the sum.
Takashi Negishi proved that, under certain assumptions, every Pareto efficient allocation maximizes such a weighted sum for some set of positive weights.

title: Kaldor–Hicks efficiency

definition.text: A change counts as a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if the people who gain could, in principle, fully compensate the people who lose, even if they never actually do.

facts.text: It is a looser test than a Pareto improvement, useful because almost any real policy change makes at least one person worse off.
Every Pareto improvement is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement, but most Kaldor–Hicks improvements are not Pareto improvements.
Example: a deal that causes pollution is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if buyers and sellers would still go ahead while fully compensating the pollution's victims.
The Kaldor test asks whether gainers would pay enough to win losers' consent; the Hicks test asks whether losers could not afford to bribe gainers to drop the change.
It is named after the twentieth-century economists Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks.
It underpins cost–benefit analysis: approving a project when benefits exceed costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers.
Critics ask why the mere ability to compensate losers should matter morally if compensation is never paid, and note that it ignores income distribution.
The Kaldor–Hicks compensation principle is the standard criterion in cost–benefit analysis of climate change.

contested_note: Critics dispute why hypothetical compensation that is never paid should carry moral weight in deciding policy.

title: Distributive justice

definition.text: The question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members.

facts.text: Distributive justice looks at outcomes, in contrast with fair process and formal equal opportunity.
Most modern theories of distributive justice start from the fact that material resources are scarce.
Leading theories include Rawls's justice as fairness, utilitarianism, egalitarianism and Marxism's 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'.
In an environmental setting it means sharing a society's environmental risks, harms and benefits fairly; such burdens fall mostly on the Global South while benefits go mainly to the Global North.
In climate justice, distributive justice asks who bears the costs of climate change and of the actions taken against it.
Friedrich von Hayek called distributive justice meaningless in a market system, where outcomes arise spontaneously rather than by anyone's design.
Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that the term is not neutral, because no central distributor hands out shares.

contested_note: Theorists hold widely different conceptions of distributive justice, and libertarians such as Hayek and Nozick reject the idea itself.

definition.text: The different rules a group can use to share out rewards and costs, such as equal shares, shares by contribution, or shares by need.

facts.text: Donelson R. Forsyth defines five norms: equality, equity, power, need and responsibility.
Under equality everyone gets the same share whatever they put in; under equity people who contribute more receive more.
Members of large groups prefer to share rewards and costs according to equity.
Under the need norm, those in greatest need get more resources regardless of what they contributed.

definition.text: John Rawls's theory, set out in A Theory of Justice, that a just society gives equal rights and liberties, equal opportunity, and arranges inequalities to benefit the least advantaged.

facts.text: Rawls roots justice in society's 'basic structure', the fundamental rules that shape its institutions and so its citizens' life chances.
The first principle, the liberty principle, gives everyone equal access to basic rights and liberties.
The second principle, the difference principle, allows inequalities only if they bring the greatest benefit to the least advantaged and positions stay open to all.

definition.text: The view, based on the equal worth of all people, that citizens should be treated equally in respect and concern by the state and by one another.

facts.text: Egalitarianism focuses on unchosen circumstances that hold people back, and its central problem is deciding which kind of equality to pursue.
Strict egalitarianism insists on equal shares even when an unequal split would make everyone better off, so it can produce Pareto-inefficient outcomes.
Equality of welfare concerns outcomes; critics favour equality of prospects instead, such as equality of opportunity.
